attribution: Part of the Markandeya Purana; author unknown
period: Commonly dated to around the 5th–7th centuries CE
summary: A Sanskrit hymn-narrative of 13 chapters, also called Durga Saptashati or Chandi, praising the Goddess as the supreme power who defeats the demons.
whyRead: It is often described as the first text to present the Goddess as the supreme reality in a sustained way. It is recited widely, especially during Navaratri.
story: A dispossessed king and a merchant betrayed by his family meet a sage, Medhas, and ask why they still feel attached. He answers by telling three stories of the Goddess defeating demons: Madhu and Kaitabha, Mahishasura, and Shumbha and Nishumbha.
questions: Is the ultimate reality a Goddess?
Why does attachment persist even when we know better?

keyTeachings.title: The Goddess as supreme
keyTeachings.text: The Devi is presented as the power (shakti) behind creation, preservation and dissolution, and as the source of the powers of the gods.

keyTeachings.title: Both binding and liberating
keyTeachings.text: The Goddess is described both as the great illusion (mahamaya) that binds beings and as the one who grants liberation when pleased.

keyTeachings.title: Protection of the world
keyTeachings.text: She manifests whenever the world is threatened, a promise echoing the Gita's theme of divine descent.

structure.label: Place in the Purana
structure.note: Markandeya Purana, commonly counted as chapters 81–93

passages.about: The three episodes of the Goddess's victories

relatedTexts.note: Its theme of divine protection parallels Gita 4.7–8
